papers.title: Replicate libraries set the noise floor for cell-state claims in cross-sectional single-cell data: an empirical audit in drug-tolerant EGFR-mutant PC9 cells
papers.abstract: Claims that drug-tolerant cancer cells occupy stable states rest on single-cell snapshots with one sequencing library per condition, where a difference between conditions cannot be separated from a difference between libraries. No standard says how far a contrast must exceed replicate-library variation. We contribute a replicate-referenced framework: a distance ratio expressing a contrast as a multiple of the distance between replicate libraries of one condition, and a library-level permutation test giving exact p values by relabelling whole libraries. In simulations, single-library tests and a split-half reference rejected a true null in 99 to 100% of runs, and Harmony followed by a cell-level test did so in 12 to 32% with structured library effects. With four libraries per arm, the library-level test held false positives at 3 to 5% in every setting. In public osimertinib-treated PC9 data with two libraries per condition (GSE150949), halves of one library were indistinguishable, replicate libraries separated at 59 to 93% accuracy, and contrasts between times in drug and sort gates exceeded replicate distance 4.5- to 51-fold. In Drop-seq erlotinib data with one library per condition (GSE149383), two libraries of the same condition separated more readily (93.3%) than withdrawn and re-treated cells (88.5%). Cross-sectional contrasts should be reported as multiples of replicate-library distance and, with four or more libraries per arm, tested by library-level permutation. Cells moved away from the untreated profile and stayed away, but the data do not support attractor-style inference, nor do they show that tolerant states are not bistable.

papers.title: Resident liver macrophages buffer dietary and circulating cholesterol to maintain hepatocyte homeostasis

papers.title: Rapid enhancement of antibiotic resistance and divergent remodeling of gene expression in single cells of bacteria

papers.title: Multimodal population-scale cell atlases define archetypes and extremes of human blood
papers.abstract: The cellular composition of blood is fundamental to human physiology and is routinely measured to assess health and disease. papers.title: Single-cell dissection of immune-state architecture across diverse human population cohorts
papers.abstract: The extension of human lifespan is accompanied by a growing burden of chronic disease and multimorbidity. The immune system, whose functional state is continuously remodelled by ageing, environmental exposures, infection history and disease, is pivotal to respond to these challenges. Disentangling of genetic and clinical influences reveals coordinated regulatory programmes associated with metabolic, inflammatory and infectious remodelling. These programmes are observed in specific disease contexts and immune states, such as those induced by chronic viral exposure, often independently of genetic differences. Together, our findings support a model of immune-state architecture shaped by ageing, environment, disease history and genetic variation, which can be read from population-specific regulatory landscapes.

papers.title: Hierarchical genetic regulatory architecture of the human immune system informs complex disease mechanisms
papers.abstract: How inherited genetic variation propagates through multicellular regulatory systems to influence human disease remains poorly understood. papers.abstract: Compromised myogenic repair with enhanced fibrosis is common in myopathies, including Wooden Breast (WB) myopathy in broilers, but the underlying mechanism of their co-occurrence remains elusive. papers.title: Primary sclerosing cholangitis: epidemiology, risk factors, pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnosis, and management.
papers.abstract: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a rare cholangiopathy characterized by multifocal inflammation and fibrostenotic remodeling of the bile ducts, cholestasis, and increased risks of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer. No pharmacological therapy has yet improved transplant-free survival. Clinical care therefore depends on accurate phenotyping, surveillance, treatment of biliary and intestinal complications, and timely liver transplantation. Population-based and clinical studies define the epidemiology, risk factors, presentation, diagnosis, and management of PSC. Studies of human biospecimens, including microbiome and metabolomic analyses, describe biological changes associated with the disease, whereas organoid and animal models are used to investigate potential mechanisms. The available evidence links genetic susceptibility and PSC-associated inflammatory bowel disease to cholangiocyte injury, immune activation, disturbed bile acid homeostasis, and microbial alterations. At the bile duct interface, cholangiocyte senescence and barrier dysfunction may interact with microbial exposure and immune-cell recruitment to promote periductal fibrosis. PSC is therefore more plausibly viewed as a multicellular process than as the consequence of a single microbial, immune, or bile acid pathway. Whether dysbiosis and altered bile acid profiles contribute to disease development or instead reflect established PSC remains unresolved. Concomitant inflammatory bowel disease, medication use, biliary obstruction, and previous biliary interventions further complicate causal inference. Longitudinal human studies may distinguish early drivers from secondary changes. Mechanistic findings should ultimately improve patient phenotyping, surveillance, endoscopic management, and selection for targeted trials. Such trials will require biologically informed designs and endpoints that capture durable clinical benefit.

papers.title: Acid-sensing ion channels in pain and psychiatric disorders: from basic properties to comorbidity mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that mediate Na+ and Ca2+ influx upon activation by extracellular acidification. Beyond protons, endogenous ligands, toxins, and small molecules modulate ASIC gating through direct or synergistic mechanisms. ASICs have emerged as key players in pain and psychiatric disorders. Tissue acidosis drives hyperalgesia via sustained ASIC activation, synaptic plasticity disruption, and central sensitization, thereby promoting chronic pain. In limbic circuits, ASIC1a expression in the amygdala, periaqueductal gray, and dorsal raphe nucleus links these channels to anxiety and depression, with ASIC1a antagonists demonstrating robust efficacy in preclinical models. Selective ASIC modulators represent promising therapeutic candidates for pain-psychiatric comorbidities. This review integrates ASIC biophysical properties with their molecular and circuit-level mechanisms in disease, offering a framework to guide future translational efforts targeting ASIC-mediated pathologies.

papers.title: Spatial causal discovery reveals novel mechanisms of cellular senescence in human liver
papers.abstract: The complex network of mechanisms that surround cellular senescence, such as its precise causes and effects, are not entirely understood at present. Senescence occurs when a cell permanently ceases dividing, halts apoptosis, stops performing its normal functions, and begins secreting chemicals that can induce other cells in its environment to also become senescent. Senescent cells are present in both healthy and unhealthy tissue, but their abundance is positively correlated with disease and age. A better understanding of senescence could lead to healthier aging, improved recovery from chemotherapy, or increased lifespan. This study used novel machine learning algorithms - with guaranteed properties of correctness under broad assumptions - to investigate senescence in human liver tissue by analyzing Visium spatial transcriptomics data. This produced data-driven models of the causes and effects of senescence, both locally and from nearby tissue. This report includes an assessment of whether the data meet key requirements for causal analysis, the transcripts identified by causal analyses as causes and effects of senescence marker genes, and pathway analyses of those gene sets. Key Takeaways 1. Senescence in Visium data from human liver tissue is spatially autocorrelated, exhibiting significant spatial clustering. 2. We show that Visium data from human liver tissue satisfies the causal Markov condition. 3. We introduce novel spatial extensions of established causal discovery machine learning algorithms and apply them on Visium data from human liver tissue. The causal modeling produced lists of transcripts directly (i) upstream and (ii) downstream of senescence marker genes, which had relatively little overlap with standard senescence marker lists SenMayo and SenUMN. 4. Pathway analyses of the upstream and downstream transcripts reveal that senescence-associated signaling integrates cellular stress inputs and immune responses to fuel a self-sustaining loop of integrin-mediated TGF-β activation and continuous matrix deposition.

papers.title: An Eight-Gene Prognostic Signature Capturing EGFR-Driven, Immune-Cold Biology in Cutaneous Melanoma
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Cutaneous melanoma remains the deadliest skin cancer despite advances in targeted therapy and immunotherapy. About 14–27% of melanomas carry mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene, and these patients have limited options once immunotherapy fails. Recent work has shown that NF1 loss drives EGFR upregulation and EGFR-dependent growth in patient-derived models, that NF1-mutant melanomas form immune-cold meta-niches with impaired antigen presentation and CD8 T cell exclusion, and that they harbor a proliferative, CDC20-dependent transcriptional program amenable to combination targeting. However, no bulk-tissue, multi-cohort gene expression signature has yet operationalized this EGFR-driven, immune-cold biology in association with clinical outcomes, and it remains unknown whether such a signature tracks with NF1 mutation status or captures a broader EGFR-driven phenotype. Methods: From 242 NF1/RAS pathway genes, we built a signature using TCGA-SKCM bulk RNA-seq. WGCNA identified genes co-expressed with NF1; LASSO Cox regression selected the final signature. We evaluated it in four independent GEO cohorts and characterized its biology with GSVA, immune deconvolution, and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE72056), and assessed associations with NF1 mutation status and clinical features. Results: The final 8-gene signature (PLA2G2D, FASLG, RASGRP1, FLT3, FGF1, PLA2G5, FGF2, EGFR) stratified patients into High and Low Risk groups with significantly different overall survival (log-rank p = 1.4×10⁻¹⁰). EGFR was the only risk-factor gene (coefficient = +0.118); the remaining genes were protective. The signature was independent of age and stage in multivariate Cox analysis (HR = 5.32, 95% CI 3.55–7.99, p 1), with a pooled meta-analysis HR of 2.25 (95% CI 1.03–4.89, p = 0.041; I² = 7.6%). It did not correlate with NF1 mutation status (p = 0.12; n = 72), consistent with the possibility that the signature captures a broader EGFR-driven phenotype rather than NF1 loss per se. This analysis was underpowered to detect a modest association. Conclusions: We present a bulk-tissue 8-gene signature that operationalizes the EGFR-driven, immune-cold biology recently defined mechanistically, spatially, and therapeutically in NF1 mutant melanoma. The signature captures a broader EGFR-driven phenotype that is not restricted to NF1-mutant tumors, as it did not correlate with NF1 mutation status in our cohort. It stratifies survival in TCGA-SKCM, is independent of stage, captures an immune-cold phenotype concordant with spatial findings, and is directionally consistent in external cohorts. These findings generate testable hypotheses for selecting patients for EGFR inhibitor and immunotherapy combinations and provide a bulk-computable biomarker for prospective testing. The signature is not yet a validated clinical assay, but it is a biologically anchored, hypothesis generating tool that operationalizes the EGFR-driven, immune-cold phenotype and is immediately testable in existing RNA-seq cohorts.

papers.title: Spectrast: a multiscale spatial statistics toolkit for single-cell spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics resolves gene expression in tissue context, but the neighborhood statistics used to quantify spatial organization scale poorly to imaging-based datasets with hundreds-of-thousands of cells and thousands of genes. We recast the standard spatial-autocorrelation statistics as convolutions on a rasterized expression lattice and evaluate them with the fast Fourier transform, giving a single engine whose cost is governed by the neighborhood radius rather than the cell count. The engine computes each statistic across a continuous range of spatial scales from one shared transform, extends naturally to a differential test of spatial reorganization between tissue states, and runs unchanged on multicore CPUs or GPUs.

papers.title: Digital cytometry of immune cell types from dried blood microsamples
papers.abstract: Enumeration of circulating immune cells is an established clinical practice implemented across a plethora of indications. While flow cytometry is the gold standard for this task, cellular deconvolution algorithms provide a robust computational alternative using molecular data. These digital cytometry pipelines typically rely on millilitre-scale venous blood samples. Here, we evaluated the potential of capillary blood microsampling as a patient-centric and minimally invasive approach for the digital cytometry of major lymphocyte populations (T cells, B cells, and natural killer cells; TBNK). In a cohort of 200 participants, we compared RNA sequencing based deconvolution performance between matched PAXgene-stabilised venous blood and Mitra capillary blood microsamples. While venous transcriptomes enabled highly accurate TBNK estimation, patient-matched capillary microsamples exhibited a significant reduction in deconvolution accuracy. Computational adaptations, including the integration of capillary-specific single-cell reference profiles, yielded only limited improvements. Instead, our analyses revealed that the performance deficit was primarily driven by the decreased transcriptome complexity of the capillary microsample libraries. This study highlights the critical role of transcript diversity for cellular deconvolution and reveals the current pre-analytical challenges that must be overcome to harness transcriptomics based digital cytometry using dried blood microsamples.

papers.title: Aging drives senescence in visceral adipose to a greater extent than obesity, instigating multicellular common signaling patterns that impair organ function and drive inflammation
papers.abstract: Obesity accelerates key hallmarks of biological aging in visceral adipose tissue (VAT), yet age-associated changes in cellular senescence against a background of sustained elevated adiposity remain poorly understood. papers.title: Classification of brain tumors using pseudobulk spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Abstract Transcriptomic classification of central nervous system (CNS) tumors is emerging as a diagnostic adjunct. However, conventional bulk sequencing requires multiple tissue sections, which is challenging when biopsy material is limited or diffuse infiltration dilutes the neoplastic signal. In cases with low kNN confidence, tumor-cluster enrichment improved concordance from 60% to 76%. Pseudobulk aggregation of spatial transcriptomics data from a single tissue section can therefore yield diagnostically informative classifications using existing classifiers, with potential for tissue-limited specimens and infiltrative tumors.

papers.title: THiRST: Computer Vision Empowered Three-Dimensional High-Resolution Spatial Transcriptomics Analytics
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) preserves gene expression within tissue architecture but remains limited to individual two-dimensional (2D) sections, restricting analysis of continuous three-dimensional (3D) structures and cross-section consistency. papers.title: SpaAxFormer: Fine-Grained Token Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Axial Transformers
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics combines gene-expression measurements with spatial relationships between cells. We investigate how spatial context can be incorporated into gene-resolved representations while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence. SpaAxFormer is a spatially constrained factorized formulation that maintains contextual cell–gene states throughout the encoder. It first contextualizes genes within each cell and then exchanges corresponding-gene states across spatial neighbors, while a separate CLS representation provides a cell-level summary. Contextual gene states support gene-expression reconstruction, while CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive learning provide complementary supervision for the cell-level representation. We evaluate SpaAxFormer on gene-expression imputation and spatial-domain identification across multiple spatial-transcriptomics technologies. Compared with the included baselines, imputation results were most favorable on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) datasets and more mixed on additional technologies, while post-hoc spatial refinement consistently improved mean ARI on the Visium spatial-domain datasets where it was applied. In a single-slice component-addition analysis, mean clustering ARI increased as CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive supervision were added. Together, these results show that the same gene-resolved formulation can support complementary gene-level prediction and cell-level spatial representation while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence.

papers.abstract: In recent years, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell–Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat . papers.title: The ovarian cellular ecosystem in polycystic ovary syndrome: from cellular heterogeneity to clinical relevance.
papers.abstract: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most biologically heterogeneous disorders in reproductive endocrinology, extending far beyond the classical features of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. Although substantial progress has been made in defining the endocrine, metabolic, genetic, epigenetic, and inflammatory mechanisms associated with PCOS, these processes have largely been investigated independently, and their contribution to the marked clinical and biological heterogeneity of the disorder remains incompletely understood. Recent advances in cellular-resolution biology, including single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial omics, and multimodal molecular profiling, together with computational systems biology, enable increasingly detailed characterization of cellular states, spatial organization, and molecular relationships within the ovarian-follicular environment. In this Review, we use the ovarian cellular ecosystem as an operational systems framework to test whether PCOS-associated abnormalities observed in individual ovarian and follicular compartments form reproducible higher-order patterns of multicellular organization. The framework is organized across five measurable domains: cellular composition and states, intercellular signaling relationships, spatial niche organization, cross-compartment molecular coupling, and systemic-ovarian coupling. Current direct human cellular-resolution evidence remains sparse and compartment-specific. Available studies support altered molecular and cellular states within selected ovarian and follicular compartments more strongly than coordinated, spatially organized, or progressive ecosystem-wide remodeling. We critically evaluate how cellular-resolution, spatial, multi-omics, computational and artificial intelligence approaches can be used to test these ecosystem-level hypotheses, explicitly distinguishing direct measurement from computational inference and identifying the validation required for functional or causal interpretation. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of this framework for biologically informed patient stratification, ecosystem-derived biomarker discovery, mechanism-informed therapeutic development, and precision reproductive endocrinology. By integrating current evidence within a falsifiable framework, this Review defines measurable features and validation criteria for testing ovarian ecosystem organization in PCOS and identifies the critical evidence gaps that future cellular-resolution, spatial, and multi-omic studies must address. This provides a practical roadmap for determining whether reproducible ovarian ecosystem states can improve biological stratification, biomarker discovery, or therapeutic target identification beyond compartment-specific abnormalities and established systemic and clinical determinants.

papers.title: Fibrotic Scars and the Potential Therapeutics After Spinal Cord Injury.
papers.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) affects millions of people worldwide, resulting in persistent direct and secondary effects including but not limited to motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction. The widespread nature of this condition, as well as its detrimental effects, makes recovery following SCI an important clinical problem. One primary issue identified in SCI among other neurological conditions is fibrotic scarring, as its dynamic nature provides both beneficial and detrimental effects over its developmental course. Initially, early scar formation contributes to wound closure and tissue stabilization, but chronic, persistent fibrosis later interferes with axonal growth and other neural repair mechanisms. The scar itself is highly dynamic, consisting of components including collagens, fibronectin, proteoglycans, and laminins, all of which have diverse localization and functionality throughout scar maturation. Its formation is regulated by various signaling mechanisms, including inflammatory signaling, profibrotic pathways, vascular responses, interactions between fibroblasts and neighboring cells, and changes in the specific mechanical environment of the injury site. This review focuses primarily on SCI, with findings from additional central nervous system injury and disease models used to provide a holistic, clinically relevant overview of fibrotic scar organization, profibrotic signaling, and potential therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Angiotensin II-Induced Cardiac Fibrosis: Genomic and Molecular Drivers, Emerging Biomarkers and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Chronically elevated angiotensin II (Ang II) drives adverse cardiac remodelling, converting a reparative response into progressive interstitial and perivascular fibrosis that stiffens the ventricle and precedes overt heart failure. Acting through the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, Ang II generates reactive oxygen species, recruits and polarises immune cells and activates resident fibroblasts, converging on transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β)-dependent and mechanotransductive programmes that drive myofibroblast differentiation and excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition. The magnitude of this response varies between patients: germline variation in renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) genes, loci for heart failure and imaging-defined fibrosis, epigenomic reprogramming of the fibroblast, non-coding RNA networks and metabolic rewiring of collagen-producing cells all modulate the transition from compensated hypertrophy to fibrotic failure. This review integrates these genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic and metabolomic layers with the signalling architecture of Ang II-induced fibrosis, and reviews the circulating biomarkers-collagen turnover peptides, matricellular and immune mediators, non-coding RNAs and cell-free DNA methylation signatures-that could detect fibrotic activity before remodelling becomes irreversible. We then consider why fibrosis regression under RAAS blockade appears heterogeneous, which emerging targets are mechanistically credible, and how genotype-biomarker-imaging phenotyping could enrich antifibrotic trials. Priorities for ancestrally diverse cohorts and standardised biomarker methodology are identified.

papers.title: PLA2G2A across tumor compartments and its relevance to drug resistance.
papers.abstract: Drug resistance in cancer is shaped not only by tumor-cell-intrinsic mutations but also by spatially organized microenvironmental states. PLA2G2A, encoding group IIA secreted phospholipase A2 (sPLA2-IIA), is usually discussed as an inflammatory lipid enzyme; however, its cancer relevance depends strongly on cellular source, localization and disease stage. This Review uses a compartment-resolved framework that annotates four domains - source, spatial niche, linked biochemical output and functional or therapy-response phenotype - and separates PLA2G2A-specific mechanistic evidence from evidence for therapy or immune resistance. Several cancer studies provide PLA2G2A-specific functional evidence for invasion, proliferation/stemness, non-catalytic signaling or T-cell dysfunction, but direct demonstration that PLA2G2A changes response to a defined anticancer therapy remains sparse. The pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cancer-associated fibroblast study provides the strongest resistance-proximal immune-functional evidence, whereas mucinous colorectal extracellular vesicles, ovarian ascites, invasive-front fibroblasts, treatment-remodeled stroma and prognostic signatures require more direct therapy-response validation. Gastric and intestinal epithelial data further caution that PLA2G2A may accompany differentiation, invasion restraint, antimicrobial defense or barrier protection. We therefore argue against treating PLA2G2A as a universal oncogenic target. Instead, it should be advanced as a mechanism-matched biomarker or therapeutic hypothesis only when compartment, biochemical-output, functional and perturbational evidence converge.

papers.title: OncoSpot enables benchmarking of cancer spatial transcriptomics methods across tumor evolutionary modes
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) is increasingly used to map clonal architecture within tumors, yet methods for analyzing cancer ST data are difficult to evaluate because real tumors lack ground truth for copy-number alterations (CNAs), subclonal identity, and malignant cell fraction. OncoSpot combines a spatial evolutionary scaffold from DEMON, CNAs generated along the resulting clonal phylogeny with CNAsim, cancer-type-specific malignant transcriptional programs, and spatially clustered nonmalignant cell types, and aggregates cells into spots with known malignant fraction, subclone, and copy-number profiles. We demonstrate OncoSpot on high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, colorectal cancer, and hepatocellular carcinoma, which represent three distinct modes of tumor evolution. Simulated subclones were spatially clustered and showed stronger phylogeny–space concordance than those generated by scCube under matched subclone populations. Benchmarking CopyKAT, CancerFinder, Clonalscope, and RCTD revealed cancer-dependent performance: Clonalscope recovered copy-number signals more accurately in ovarian and colorectal cancer, whereas CopyKAT performed better in hepatocellular carcinoma, reflecting both the assumptions of each method and the copy-number landscapes of the three cancers. OncoSpot’s ground truth also exposed a failure mode in Clonalscope’s malignant spot identification, in which tumor and normal labels were inverted, and allowed us to trace its cause. These method-dependent behaviors would be difficult to detect in real data. OncoSpot provides a framework for benchmarking CNA inference, subclone detection, malignant spot identification, and normal spot deconvolution, and its modular design and guidelines allow extension to additional cancer types. OncoSpot is freely available at https://github.com/compbio-mallory/OncoSpot .

papers.title: Unified cell segmentation for spatial transcriptomics via transcript reassignment
papers.abstract: High-resolution spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression as individually localized molecules on imaging-based platforms or as counts in subcellular bins on sequencing-based platforms, and both must be assigned to cells before cell-level analysis. Existing segmentation methods focus on delineating cell boundaries, yet transcripts that diffuse beyond their cell of origin, fall where cells overlap, or lie in bins that cells only partially cover are still misassigned. Here we present Tracel, a two-stage optimal transport framework that assigns spatial observations to cells under the guidance of a matched single-cell RNA-sequencing reference. Tracel first aligns reference cells to spatial cells to estimate the expected expression profile at each cell location, and then maps transcripts to cells against these profiles. The same formulation assigns transcripts from imaging-based platforms (e.g., Xenium, CosMx) and bin counts from sequencing-based platforms (e.g., Visium HD). Across five human datasets spanning three platforms and three tissues, Tracel improves the separation of cell types over existing methods, assigning cell-type markers to their correct cells, retaining more cell-intrinsic transcripts and reducing contamination from neighboring cells. Tracel also preserves variation within cell types, yielding more accurate differential expression across spatial locations, and its expression profiles attribute ligand-receptor interactions to the correct cell-type pairs in cell-cell communication analysis. Tracel can enter the segmentation workflow at different stages, either refining an existing segmentation or segmenting cells starting from nucleus segmentation. Availability Code and example data are available at: https://tracel.readthedocs.io/en/latest/

Model-based in silico perturbation attributed the neighborhood dependency to vascular-stromal neighbors; virtual knockout of NR1H3 predicted coordinated downregulation of efferocytosis genes. Efferocytosis subprograms are thus spatially decoupled in the human infarcted myocardium, with degradation as a niche-regulated step, providing spatial and genetic leads for targeting infarct repair.

papers.title: Kontext: Kernel-based method bridging spatial domain identification and cell-cell communication
papers.abstract: The spatial organization of biological tissues is characterized by spatial domains: regions with coherent transcriptional and anatomical properties, heavily influenced by local cell-cell interactions. Although identifying spatial domains is a common task in spatial transcriptomics, most existing methods provide limited mechanistic insight into their organization. We present Kontext, a kernel-based framework that jointly represents cells and their local environments, enabling the identification of spatial domains grounded in their underlying ligand-receptor interactions. This representation further provides complementary outputs for characterizing cellular microenvironments, spatial niches, and sender-receiver communication patterns. Kontext outperforms state-of-the-art methods in recovering reference domain annotations across several spatial transcriptomics technologies and biological models, while offering improved computational efficiency and scalability. Applying Kontext on a Xenium temporal mouse heart cryoinjury dataset, we characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the injury and identify an undescribed sustained activity of the complement system in the communication between fibroblasts and macrophages during scar maturation. In a million-cell three-dimensional Open-ST dataset of human metastatic lymph node tissue, we combine spatial domain identification and niche analysis to define the boundary region between the tumor and its microenvironment, revealing distinct communication patterns between this interface and the tumor core.

papers.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals Age-Specific Cancer Hallmark Architecture in Pediatric and Adult Brain Tumors
papers.abstract: Pediatric cancers are fundamentally different from their adult counterparts. Specifically, pediatric cancers carry fewer mutations, interact with developing immune systems, and have active developmental microenvironments. We compared the spatial gene expression patterns of the Cancer Hallmarks gene sets between the TME and neoplastic compartments in pediatric brain tumors. Compared with a similar study of adult brain tumors, in which Cancer Hallmark expression patterns clearly separated the TME and neoplastic compartments, we identified three hallmarks (“Deregulating Cellular Energetics,” “Senescent Cells,” and “Evading Growth Suppressors”) whose predominant cellular compartments differed between pediatric and adult tumors. In pediatric samples, these hallmarks were associated primarily with the TME rather than the neoplastic compartment. This shift implicates an age-specific rewiring of the tumor ecosystem. We also provide clear evidence of strong transcriptomic regulation in genes shared by pediatric and adult neoplastic compartments. Finally, we show how measures of spatial autocorrelation may be used to distinguish tumor grade. Significance Distinguishing between pediatric and adult tumors is essential for tailoring treatments to specific age groups and discovering new interactions between the tumor microenvironment (TME) and neoplasms. Pediatric brain tumors exhibit distinct biological features compared to their adult counterparts, including lower mutational burden and unique immune responses. However, whether these differences manifest primarily in tumors, the TME, or both has been unclear. In this study, we systematically compare the Cancer Hallmarks architecture using existing spatial transcriptomic gene sets and ask whether each set is more frequently observed in the neoplastic compartment versus the TME of pediatric tumors. By preserving the spatial resolution of gene expression, our findings elucidate pediatric tumor pathways, genetic factors, and how these interact with surrounding tissue. This framework may clarify how age-associated developmental programs shape growth-promoting states in pediatric tumors and their TME.

papers.title: Long-read genome sequencing resolves complex structural variants in exome-negative developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
papers.abstract: Background and ObjectivesDespite standard genetic testing, approximately two-thirds of patients with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) remain undiagnosed. Pathogenic noncoding and structural variants (SVs), that are difficult to detect or resolve using short-read sequencing, may contribute to this diagnostic gap. To evaluate the diagnostic contribution of long-read genome sequencing (lrGS), we recruited a cohort of 124 families with sporadic DEE who remained unsolved by prior ES. MethodsTrio lrGS (Oxford Nanopore or PacBio HiFi) was performed, complemented by short-read genome sequencing (srGS) and mRNA sequencing (blood or fibroblast) of index cases, where available. Comprehensive variant analysis included small nucleotide variants, indels, SVs, and short tandem repeats. To identify the diagnostic yield of each method, we compared lrGS, srGS and ES re-analysis, and evaluated the additional value of RNA sequencing. ResultsWe established a diagnosis in 21 of 124 families (16.9%). Fourteen variants were retrospectively detectable in prior ES. Two cases with non-coding variants in SCN1A and RNU2-2 were detectable by both srGS and lrGS. Five SVs also required genome sequencing (5.6% of the total cohort), three of which could be detected, but not confidently resolved by srGS due to breakpoint complexity, repeat-mediated rearrangements, and large copy-neutral events: LrGS enabled accurate characterization of Alu-mediated CDKL5 and STXBP1 deletions and a MEF2C deletion with large inversion. A copy-neutral SCN1A inversion was well characterizable by both srGS and lrGS. One balanced translocation t(X;17) disrupting CDKL5 was resolved by lrGS (srGS unavailable). RNA sequencing confirmed pathogenicity of two SVs including t(X;17), the MEF2C deletion with inversion, and two CNVs. In addition, ZNF569 and ZNF570 emerged as candidate epilepsy genes from our cohort. DiscussionIn ES-negative DEE, the incremental diagnostic yield of genome sequencing was modest, while lrGS provided particular value for the structural resolution of complex rearrangements, especially those involving repetitive sequences. The finding that two-thirds of diagnoses were retrospectively detectable in prior ES highlights the substantial value of systematic reanalysis. Further gains from genome sequencing may increasingly depend on improved interpretation of non-coding variation and integration of long-read-specific information. Our findings indicate that complex SVs represent the class for which lrGS currently yields the most distinctive diagnostic information.

papers.title: Cytokine Signatures of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor Myocarditis and the Modifying Role of Clonal Hematopoiesis: A Machine-Learning and Multi-Omics Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) myocarditis affects up to 2% of patients on ICI and has up to a 50% mortality. Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) is a risk factor for ICI myocarditis. ObjectivesTo leverage a multi-omics approach to evaluate cytokines associated with ICI myocarditis, immunosuppression resistance, CHIP in ICI myocarditis and implicated pathways and cell type contributions. Methods236 cardio-oncology patients were enrolled, including 88 who were on ICI. Cytokine profiling from patients on ICI were sampled and analyzed using machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence. Single-cell multi-omics of peripheral blood from Yale (n=19), Stanford (n=25), and MGH (n=63) evaluated cell-type contributions of cytokines and implicated pathways. Validation of Yale proteomic analyses was done using the Stanford CYTOF dataset. ResultsTop features associated with ICI myocarditis included IL13, CXCL10, PDGF-A, CCL13, CCL17 and KITlg. Top KEGG pathways associated with ICI myocarditis and immunosuppression resistant ICI myocarditis included JAK-STAT signaling, IL17 signaling and lipid/atherosclerosis pathways. At the single-cell level, the consensus signals distinguishing myocarditis from non-myocarditis across cohorts was predominantly driven by module-level JAK-STAT, T-cell, and Toll-like receptor activation. Similar transcription gene programs were activated in CHIP carriers including modules implicated in the pro-inflammatory immune response, such as NF-kappa B, IL17, MAPK, and TNF pathways within CHIP cells spanning lymphoid (cytotoxic CD8+ NKT, and natural killer cells) and myeloid lineages. ConclusionsAcross cohorts, JAK-STAT signaling emerges as a convergent and potentially actionable axis in ICI myocarditis that is further amplified in CHIP carriers, supporting cytokine-guided risk stratification and JAK-STAT-directed immunosuppression as testable strategies.

papers.title: CCL17-CCR4 Signalling Attenuates Pressure Overload-Induced Cardiac Remodelling Through IGFBP6 Suppression in Cardiac Fibroblasts
papers.abstract: Background and AimsChemokines are key regulators of immune-cell trafficking, inflammation, and tissue repair in cardiovascular disease. C-C motif chemokine ligand 17 (CCL17) has been linked to adverse remodelling after myocardial infarction and neurohumoral stress, but its function during sustained mechanical pressure overload is unknown. We investigated whether CCL17 regulates ventricular remodelling through cardiac fibroblast signalling. MethodsSerum proteomic screening and myocardial and serum validation were performed in patients with aortic stenosis and healthy controls. CCL17 function was evaluated using global Ccl17 deletion and adeno-associated virus-mediated CCL17 augmentation in mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction. Cardiac transcriptomics and complementary pharmacological, small interfering RNA, and promoter-reporter experiments in cardiac fibroblasts were used to define downstream signalling. Separately, fibroblast-directed Igfbp6 silencing was used to test the functional contribution of IGFBP6 in vivo. ResultsSerum CCL17 concentrations and myocardial CCL17 abundance were increased in patients with aortic stenosis, and cardiac and circulating CCL17 increased rapidly after transverse aortic constriction. Ccl17 deletion aggravated pressure overload-induced systolic dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibrosis, whereas CCL17 augmentation conferred reciprocal protection. Transcriptomic analyses identified insulin-like growth factor-binding protein 6 (IGFBP6) as a CCL17-responsive candidate. In cardiac fibroblasts, CCL17 reduced secreted and cellular IGFBP6 and -smooth muscle actin through C-C chemokine receptor 4 (CCR4)-dependent signalling associated with suppression of early growth response 1 (EGR1). Genetic perturbation and promoter-reporter analyses further supported CCR4-EGR1-dependent regulation of Igfbp6. Finally, fibroblast-directed Igfbp6 silencing improved systolic function and reduced hypertrophy and fibrosis in Ccl17-deficient mice after transverse aortic constriction. ConclusionsOur findings identify CCL17 as a previously unrecognized cardioprotective factor and uncover a novel immune cell-fibroblast communication axis, whereby CCL17 restrains pressure overload-induced maladaptive cardiac remodelling through CCR4-EGR1-mediated suppression of IGFBP6 in cardiac fibroblasts. papers.title: Integrative Analysis of Nucleotide Metabolism-Related Genes Reveals a Diagnostic Signature and In Silico Functional Disruption in Hypertrophic Scarring.
papers.abstract: Hypertrophic scar (HTS) is a fibrotic skin disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix accumulation and chronic inflammation. This study aimed to investigate cellular heterogeneity, immune alterations, and nucleotide metabolism-related biomarkers in HTS and to explore their potential mechanisms. Bulk transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were used for differential expression analysis, and machine learning algorithms were applied to develop a diagnostic model. Sixteen cell clusters were identified, with macrophages showing prominent activation of nucleotide metabolism pathways and immune-related signaling. The optimal Enet + svmLinear model achieved strong predictive performance (area under the curve = 0.934), and Shapley Additive exPlanations analysis identified NCF1 and GPR34 as key predictive genes. These genes were also associated with immune cell infiltration. In vitro validation using THP-1-derived M2 macrophages showed that NCF1 and GPR34 promoted transforming growth factor-β1 secretion and enhanced fibroblast activation, while their knockdown reduced α-smooth muscle actin and collagen I expression. Collectively, this study reveals the important role of macrophage-associated nucleotide metabolism in HTS and identifies NCF1 and GPR34 as potential biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Decoding the lymphangioleiomyomatosis niche microenvironment via integrative analysis of single cell multiomics and spatial transcriptomics.
papers.abstract: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare, destructive lung disease caused by mutations in tuberous sclerosis complex 1 (TSC1) or TSC2, leading to mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) hyperactivation. While mTOR inhibitor sirolimus, the only US Food and Drug Administration approved drug for this disease, stabilises lung function in most LAM patients, the drug does not eliminate LAM cells, underscoring a critical gap in our understanding of the tumour microenvironment and cellular heterogeneity that drive disease progression. This study provides the first comprehensive multiomics atlas of the human LAM niche, integrating single-cell/single-nucleus RNA-sequencing, single-nucleus ATAC-sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics to deconvolute its complex architecture. We elucidate LAM cellular heterogeneity by identifying three distinct subtypes: the canonical, uterine smooth muscle-like, mTORC1-hyperactive LAMCORE1; a novel, fibroblast-like LAMCORE2 subtype with potent extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling activity; and LAMCORE3, a substate of LAMCORE1 that shares LAM and myogenic signatures, but is characterised by lower transcriptional activity and specific functional enrichment in protein translation. Our analysis reveals the transcriptomic heterogeneity of the LAM subtypes, orchestrated by distinct transcriptional drivers and networks. Furthermore, we uncover spatially resolved LAM-associated fibroblast (LAF) states, LAF-seed and LAF-niche, that coordinate transforming growth factor-β signalling, ECM deposition and remodelling, and niche expansion. Spatial mapping uncovers a structured ecosystem where LAMCORE1 cells form a central core enmeshed with the lymphatic endothelium, which is surrounded by LAFs, LAMCORE2 cells, and reprogrammed immune and epithelial cells. Findings were validated through multimodal imaging technologies. Present work advances the field by providing the first high-resolution blueprint of the LAM niche microenvironment, revealing novel cell states and crosstalk that identify promising novel therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Perineural Invasion Is Associated With Stromal Remodeling, Angiogenesis, and Neural Features in Colorectal Cancer.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPerineural invasion (PNI) is known as a pathological indicator of aggressive tumor behavior and is associated with poor survival in colorectal cancer (CRC). Although individual biological features associated with PNI have been reported, the relationship between PNI and neural cell attraction and stromal features within the tumor microenvironment remains incompletely understood. We aimed to characterize the clinical, genomic, immune, stromal, vascular, and neural features associated with PNI-positive CRC.MethodsClinical and transcriptomic data from 179 CRC patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) were analyzed. PNI status was morphologically determined from pathological records, yidlding 45 PNI-positive and 134 PNI-negative cases. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using Hallmark gene sets characterized transcriptomic differences. Genomic features, immune cell composition, consensus molecular subtypes (CMS), stromal and vascular features, and neural features were compared between groups.ResultsPNI-positive CRC was associated with advanced T category, distant metastasis, advanced stage, and worse progression-free survival. There was the enrichment of proliferation-related pathways, including E2F targets, the G2M checkpoint and MYC target pathways, in PNI-positive CRC. However, genomic differences were limited, with higher homologous recombination deficiency and TP53 mutation frequency in PNI-positive CRC. PNI was not associated with broad changes in xCell immune scores but showed reduced interferon-α and interferon-γ responses. PNI-positive CRC was enriched in the mesenchymal consensus molecular subtype 4 (CMS4) and showed increased stromal fraction and extracellular matrix gene expression. Vascular features were also increased, including endothelial cells and lymphatic endothelial cells, together with enrichment of angiogenesis and increased transforming growth factor (TGF)-β-related features. Notably, PNI-positive CRC showed increased Schwann cell and neuron projection guidance scores and higher expression of axon guidance genes. These findings identified concurrent stromal, vascular, and neural features associated with PNI-positive CRC.ConclusionsPNI-positive CRC is characterized by a coordinated mesenchymal and stromal phenotype accompanied by angiogenic and neural features, with relatively limited genomic and immune differences. These findings provide a biological framework that may help explain the aggressive clinical behavior of PNI-positive CRC.

papers.title: A cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas reveals intra- and intercellular signaling in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) arises from pathological interactions among diverse brain cell types, but cell-type-specific proteomic changes remain underexplored. Here, we present deep proteomic profiling of sorted or proximity-labeled brain cells from AD mouse models (5xFAD and AppNL-G-F) at multiple ages, quantifying 13,411 proteins in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursor cells, and neurons, with additional spatial information. We identified 3,028 differentially abundant proteins, most of which were absent in a bulk proteomic dataset, and constructed cell-type-specific networks to define functional modules and hub proteins. Comparison with transcriptomic data revealed that ∼30% of proteomic changes are RNA discordant. Further analyses uncovered cross-cell-type signaling proteins conserved in human AD brains, such as pleiotrophin (Ptn), which is transcriptionally enriched in astrocytes but accumulates in microglia. Importantly, recombinant PTN activates human induced microglia (iMG) cells. Thus, these findings provide a comprehensive cell-type-resolved proteomic atlas of AD models, highlighting novel intra- and intercellular signaling events.

papers.title: Natural product integrated metal-organic frameworks for chronic wound healing: From pathological signal responsiveness to on-demand drug delivery.
papers.abstract: Natural products (NPs) possess remarkable structural diversity and broad biological activities, giving them substantial potential in chronic wound therapy. However, unfavorable physicochemical properties and poorly controlled local exposure often limit their therapeutic performance. Integrating NPs with metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) offers benefits beyond improved drug delivery. NPs can be encapsulated as cargo, incorporated as coordinating ligands, or immobilized on MOF surfaces, while natural macromolecules may themselves form bioactive dressing matrices. Thus, the key issue is not only which NP is incorporated, but also how its material role affects bioavailability and stage-specific therapeutic function. Centered on NPs, this review establishes a framework for understanding MOF-based wound therapies and explains how NP chemistry and material roles govern responsiveness to endogenous pathological signals or external physical stimuli. These effects are further linked to the changing needs of chronic wound healing, from early control of microbial burden and persistent inflammation to tissue regeneration and extracellular matrix remodeling. By moving beyond the conventional view of NPs as passive cargo, this review provides a unified design rationale for stage-adaptive NP-MOF biomaterials and bioactive dressings.

papers.title: Cellular senescence in skin inflammation: molecular mechanisms and potential clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence is increasingly regarded as a mechanism linking chronic tissue stress to persistent skin inflammation. Senescent cells are defined by stable cell-cycle arrest with remodeling of morphology, metabolism, and secretory phenotype, of which the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) is central. Because no single marker is sufficient, senescence in skin requires multiparameter, cell-type-resolved criteria. This Review addresses stress sensing, SASP induction, paracrine propagation, immune evasion, cellular heterogeneity, and therapeutic targeting, stratifying evidence by disease: chronic and diabetic wounds are best supported, whereas in psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, and vitiligo the evidence remains largely associative, as SASP-like mediators overlap with cytokine programs from activated keratinocytes, stromal cells, and immune cells. Senescence-targeted interventions are classified as senolytics, senomorphics, or senopreventive/geroprotective strategies, and assessed at marker, SASP, senescent-cell-burden, and disease-outcome levels. It further notes that clinical translation depends on defining senescence-maintained lesion subtypes, establishing combinatorial biomarkers and spatial maps, and validating the efficacy and safety window of local therapies in suitable models and human tissues.

papers.title: Advanced Cellular Models for Drug Testing and Discovery to Target Cardiac Fibrosis Progression.
papers.abstract: Cardiac fibrosis is a complex and dynamic pathological process, central for cardiac repair, characterised by continuous cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. Three-dimensional (3D) models are gaining increasing relevance, compared with traditional two-dimensional (2D) cellular setups, due to their ability to recapitulate key features of the fibrotic microenvironment at different levels of complexity, including cellular heterogeneity, spatial organisation and tissue mechanical properties. These systems have enabled a deeper investigation of fibrosis mechanobiology and the mechanosensitive pathways involved in disease progression, contributing to the identification of potential therapeutic targets for cardiac repair. Increasing biological complexity can reveal therapeutic responses that remain undetected in conventional models; however, the predictive value of 3D systems has so far been confirmed in vivo only for a limited number of platforms and compounds. papers.title: From Fixed Lineage to Dynamic States: Fibro-Adipogenic Progenitors in Skeletal Muscle Regeneration, Fibrosis, and Fibrofatty Degeneration.

papers.title: Multiomics Reveals a Production Signature Resembling Mammalian Metabolic Ageing and That Dietary Spermidine Enhances Lipid Handling in Farmed Salmon.
papers.abstract: Metabolic ageing and associated changes in lipid mobilisation have been heavily studied in humans and model taxa, yet remain poorly understood in farmed animals, with potentially important implications for health and welfare outcomes. Importantly, this occurred in parallel to changes in lipid and protein markers that may reprogram lipid handling, supporting a hypothesis that spermidine supplementation counters the proposed metabolic ageing related phenotype. As farmed salmon exhibit multiple features of human metabolic ageing linked to its recent domestication, this species offers a novel model for vertebrate ageing studies.

papers.title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units—cells, bins or multicellular spots—into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p -values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene–gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p -values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.

papers.title: Dysregulated B Cell Education Drives Autoimmunity and Immunodeficiency in Down Syndrome
papers.abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) present with both increased rates of autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. papers.title: Redefining Synovial Pathotypes in Psoriatic Arthritis through Multi-Modal Histology and Machine Learning (The PSYNOVIUM Study)

Whole-slide digital image analysis and automated pixel classifiers quantified cellular and stromal metrics. Unsupervised hierarchical clustering identified intrinsic PsA pathotypes, which were correlated with clinical disease activity, radiographic osteoarthritis (OA), and longitudinal treatment responses. Pathotypes were independent of treatment and concurrent radiographic knee OA. The Fibro-Stromal pathotype correlated with significantly higher cutaneous psoriasis severity. Longitudinally, patients with the Fibro-Stromal pathotype exhibited a trend toward lower treatment response (44%) following standard interventions (methotrexate or TNF inhibitors) compared to the Dense Myeloid (50%) and Angio-Lymphoid (80%) pathotypes. InterpretationWe present the first computationally derived synovial pathotypes specific to PsA, revealing distinct plasma cell and fibrotic architectures not captured by RA-centric models. To enable clinical translation, we distilled these findings into a pragmatic, four-marker diagnostic decision tree (CD31, CD68, CD138, and picrosirius red) designed for routine histopathology workflows, providing a staging ground for biomarker-stratified clinical trials in PsA. However, psoriatic arthritis (PsA) exhibits a fundamentally distinct synovial microenvironment, characterised by unique vascular architecture, altered stromal fibroblast phenotypes, and distinct immune infiltrates intertwined with the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine axis. papers.title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
papers.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analysed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

papers.title: A Centripetal Antigen‐Sequestration Niche in the Sarcoidosis Granuloma Without Consistent Recruitment of Homeostatic CD10+ Macrophages
papers.abstract: Background: The granuloma is the defining lesion of sarcoidosis, yet the internal architecture of the non-necrotising lesion — and whether the homeostatic CD10/MME+ macrophage identity enters it — is unresolved in lung. Objectives: To map the programme-level spatial anatomy of the sarcoidosis granuloma and test prespecified cross-disease predictions. Methods: We analysed 10x Visium spatial transcriptomes of three sarcoidosis lungs and one healthy control (GSE262998), four TSC1/2-deficient granuloma-model mouse lungs (GSE263088) and two validation cohorts (nine explanted sarcoidosis lungs, GSE288607; four tuberculous granuloma sections, GSE296400). Granuloma spots, partitioned into core, rim, mid and far zones, were scored for 25 macrophage modules and 49 convergence signatures. Results: A quadripartite programme — antigen presentation (core 1.48–1.80 vs 1.02–1.28), iron handling (1.30–1.45 vs 0.68–1.22), lysosomal mass (0.69–0.95 vs 0.19–0.51), cell fusion (+0.07 to +0.22 core−far in 3/3 sections) — peaked at the core in all three sarcoidosis sections, while hypoxia was flat, unlike the hypoxic-necrotic tuberculosis archetype; the gradients survived density matching, and deconvolution attributed 59–74% of core elevations to per-spot macrophage content (i.e., 26–41% of the elevations reflect per-cell state change rather than composition). The CD10/MME+ identity was not consistently recruited (core MME 0.22 versus 0.38 at far in one section; weak, inconsistent enrichment in two). All four programmes replicated across 80 sarcoidosis nodules (median Δz +0.20 to +0.52; hypoxia +0.03); tuberculous caseous cores displayed perinecrotic hypoxia cuffs with fusion depleted in the caseum (and not enriched in the viable cuff), and the prespecified foam check was falsified (sarcoidosis-strong). Conclusions: The sarcoidosis granuloma is a centripetally organised, perfusion-preserving antigen-sequestration niche without hypoxia; the homeostatic CD10+ identity is not a consistent niche component.

papers.title: Agentic AI enables cell segmentation-free cell-type inference and cell-type-guided cell segmentation in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell-type identification in spatial transcriptomics often relies on cell segmentation, which can introduce inaccuracies in cell boundaries and transcript assignment. Segmentation-free or cell-free methods have been developed to completely avoid cell segmentation, but inaccurate cell typing hinder accurate downstream analysis. Here, we introduce SSAF-T, a segmentation-free agentic framework that identifies cell types directly from spatial gene expression without predefined reference datasets. For the reference-free cell typing, SSAF-T incorporates CeLLMan, which employs expert-level agents for each organ to annotate cell types using a literature-grounded knowledge graph. We benchmark SSAF-T on both array-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics datasets in terms of accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. We further show that SSAF-T provides an accurate cell segmentation based on the segmentation-free mapping, which ensure compatibility to existing downstream analysis ecosystem, and eventually enable quantitative analysis at single-cell level.

papers.title: Spatially Resolved Immunometabolic Reprogramming of Tumor-Associated Macrophages: An Integrative Multi-Layer Re-Analysis of Public Spatial Metabolomics, Spatial Transcriptomics and Single-Cell Resources
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolic reprogramming of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) drives tumor immune evasion, yet the spatial and subtype-level organization of TAM metabolism remains under-characterized. Methods: We re-analyzed public spatial metabolomics, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell datasets using autocorrelation-corrected spatial statistics, patient-level testing, and replication across breast, lung, colorectal, liver, and brain tumor data. Results: TAMs formed the most spatially clustered transcriptional module in breast tumor sections. TAM-dense regions were robustly coupled to iron handling (ρ = 0.568), surviving gene-overlap, cell-abundance, and erythrocyte/vascular-exposure controls, whereas apparent glycolysis and lipid-uptake links did not survive spatial or abundance correction. In lung adenocarcinoma, subtype comparisons were confounded by tissue origin; within tumor tissue, two differences persisted across patients (higher lipid uptake in C1QC⁺ and higher iron handling in FOLR2⁺ TAMs). A reported SPP1⁺-versus-C1QC⁺ polarity recurred at cell level across cancer types but not at patient level. Mitochondrial DNA tracing detected clonally expanded, metabolically hyperactive TAMs in two of four evaluable samples. Conclusions: TAM metabolism is spatially organized and subtype-specific, with iron handling as the most robust territorial coupling, supporting spatially stratified, subtype-aware design of metabolism-targeting trials.

papers.title: DisCell: Separating Spillover from Niche Response in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics at single-cell resolution measures every cell in its place in the tissue, but diffusion and segmentation errors also add transcripts of neighboring cells to a cell’s counts. This spillover makes a cell resemble its neighbors, and a response to the niche makes cells in the same niche resemble each other. Both tie a cell’s expression to its surroundings. The count data alone cannot tell the two apart. Findings: from single-cell transcriptomes, such as a gene program that is higher in one niche than in another or signaling genes that change depending on the neighborhood, may therefore be artifacts of spillover. Current models describe a cell by its intrinsic state together with either its niche response or spillover, but none models all three. We present DisCell, the first method that models all three components jointly and measures how robust each finding is to spillover. DisCell is a generative model that describes single-cell gene expression profiles in terms of two latent variables, an intrinsic state and a response to the niche, and adds spillover from its neighbors as a separate term. DisCell fits the model at increasing levels of spillover and recomputes each finding on the spillover-free expression to see how much spillover it withstands. DisCell also estimates the most spillover a section can contain, and a finding that holds even at that amount is not explained by spillover. In simulated tissue, DisCell recovers each cell’s intrinsic state and response and tells findings created by spillover apart from genuine responses. On five sections of ovarian and lung tissue, the intrinsic state keeps more of each cell’s own properties, measured by its cell-cycle phase, than any competing method that holds as little of its neighborhood. Within each cell type, the model partitions the variation of each gene into intrinsic state, niche response and spillover. Using DisCell, we rank findings about niches by their robustness to spillover and confirm that a previously reported finding withstands spillover, that esophageal cancer cells in niches infiltrated by immune or stromal cells express more of an epithelial–mesenchymal transition program. DisCell also predicts what the gene expression of a cell type would be in another niche, with its spillover part separated, at lower error on most tasks than the competing method built for this purpose. Training the model takes under ten minutes on one consumer GPU for sections of up to 400,000 cells.

papers.title: A healthy donor kidney aging signature estimable from PAS histology and its association with progression of diabetic kidney disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundAs kidneys age, their cells change in arrangement and gene expression. Whether these changes are also present in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), and whether they relate to how quickly kidney function is lost, is not known. MethodsZero-time biopsies from 24 healthy living kidney donors (aged 36-66 years) and biopsies from 28 patients with DKD were profiled by single-cell-level spatial transcriptomics with a 5,101-gene panel. In the donors, we identified how cell neighborhoods and cell-type gene expression change with age and summarized the expression changes as tissue-aging scores. The scores were applied unchanged to DKD and related to the rate of eGFR decline after biopsy in 24 patients, with adjustment for age, sex, baseline eGFR, and proteinuria. We also estimated the scores from routine periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) slides, using models that did not include the patient being scored. ResultsIn older donors, immune cells were less often found next to tubular epithelium, and contacts between endothelial cells and podocytes and between stromal and epithelial cells were fewer, although cell proportions changed little. Expression of stress-response and cell-cycle regulators (FOXO3, CDKN1A, BBC3, PINK1, IRAK1, SOCS1) increased. Changes in cell contacts in DKD tissue largely followed the same direction as those in older donors. In DKD, higher tissue-aging scores were associated with faster eGFR loss independently of age, sex, baseline eGFR, and proteinuria (overall score, partial {rho} = -0.61); this held for tubular, endothelial, immune, and parietal epithelial cell scores but not for the podocyte score. Scores estimated from PAS slides correlated with the transcriptomic scores (mean {rho} = 0.62) and were also associated with faster eGFR loss (partial {rho}, -0.44 to -0.56). ConclusionsHealthy kidney aging involves a selective loss of cell contacts together with a coordinated stress-response program. DKD kidneys that carry this aging phenotype lose function faster, and the phenotype can be estimated in part from the routine diagnostic PAS slide.

papers.title: Matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures reveal astrocyte-centered neuroimmune alterations in Alzheimer’s disease
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Extracellular matrix remodeling and altered tissue mechanics are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but links between matrix stiffness and AD pathology remain unclear. Objective To identify matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures in AD and characterize their diagnostic potential, functions, cell-type specificity, and intercellular communication patterns. Methods Bulk transcriptomic datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus were integrated with literature-derived matrix stiffness-related genes. Differential expression analysis, three machine-learning algorithms, and cross-dataset validation were used to identify candidate genes and construct a multigene classification model. Functional enrichment and immune-cell deconvolution analyses were performed. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed to assess cell-type-specific expression, inferred astrocyte trajectories, and predicted cell–cell communication. Results Eighty-one differentially expressed matrix stiffness-related genes were identified in AD brain tissue. FREM3, DUSP4, and FAM107A were selected and showed concordant differential expression across discovery and validation datasets. The three-gene model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.963 in the discovery cohort. Gene set enrichment analysis linked all three genes to oxidative phosphorylation, although FAM107A showed an enrichment direction opposite to DUSP4 and FREM3. Immune deconvolution suggested associations with immune-cell signatures. Single-cell analysis identified astrocytes as a major population expressing the three-gene signature. AD astrocytes showed altered pseudotime distributions and stronger predicted communication with immune cells, particularly T cells and macrophages. Conclusions FREM3, DUSP4, and FAM107A are candidate matrix stiffness-related transcriptomic signatures in AD and may connect extracellular matrix remodeling with mitochondrial metabolism, immune dysregulation, and astrocyte-associated changes. Independent clinical validation and experimental confirmation are required.

papers.title: Integrated Multi-Omics and Machine Learning Identify PTTG1 as a Prognostic Biomarker and Therapeutic Target in Endometrial Cancer
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) exhibits high molecular heterogeneity, and the lack of precise prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets severely limits the clinical management of high-risk patients. This study aimed to identify a robust multi-omics biomarker and elucidate its intrinsic oncogenic mechanisms and extrinsic immune-remodeling roles in the UCEC microenvironment. Methods We systematically integrated transcriptomic data from TCGA and GEO cohorts. WGCNA coupled with four machine learning algorithms (LASSO, SVM-RFE, XGBoost, Boruta) were employed for feature selection. Single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were integrated to map the cellular landscape. In silico virtual knockout, virtual overexpression, and pharmacogenomic analyses were conducted. Computational predictions were experimentally validated using Western blot, qRT-PCR, and immunohistochemistry in paired clinical specimens, and corroborated by CPTAC proteomic analysis. Results PTTG1 was identified as an independent prognostic biomarker, with significant overexpression confirmed at both mRNA and protein levels and predominant nuclear localization in tumor epithelium. Mechanistically, virtual knockout revealed PTTG1 drives malignant progression through hyperactivation of cell cycle, ribosome biogenesis, and glutathione metabolism, whereas virtual overexpression activated immune-related transcriptional networks including MHC class II antigen presentation. Integrated scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics demonstrated PTTG1 enrichment in malignant epithelial cells and tumor-associated macrophages. Drug sensitivity predictions identified selective vulnerability to MEK inhibitors, including selumetinib and trametinib. Conclusion PTTG1 serves as a multidimensional oncogenic driver and independent prognostic biomarker in UCEC, intrinsically fueling tumor proliferation while extrinsically orchestrating an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Bidirectional in silico perturbation revealed distinct transcriptional consequences, substantiated by multi-level experimental validation. Drug sensitivity predictions identified selective MEK inhibitor vulnerabilities, providing a rationale for PTTG1-guided prognostic stratification and targeted therapeutic strategies in high-risk UCEC.

papers.title: Multi-omics analysis reveals PITX1 as a predictor of immunotherapy efficacy in clear cell renal cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved outcomes in advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), but predictive biomarkers are lacking. The role of paired-like homeodomain 1 (PITX1) in ccRCC remains unclear. Methods Machine learning identified PITX1 as a key biomarker. Results PITX1 was upregulated in ccRCC, associated with BAP1 mutation and hypomethylation. scRNA-seq and ST revealed the expression patterns of PITX1 in different cell clusters. High PITX1 expression correlated with advanced clinicopathological features, poor survival, and metabolic reprogramming towards glucose and methionine metabolism. Enrichment analysis suggested high PITX1 would lead to more malignant tumor biological behaviors. It shaped an immunosuppressive microenvironment with regulatory T cells (Tregs) infiltrated and elevated immune checkpoints. Crucially, high PITX1 indicates inferior benefits for patients receiving immunotherapy. Conclusion PITX1 is a novel biomarker linked to aggressive tumor behavior, metabolic alteration, and immune evasion, predicting poor response to immunotherapy in ccRCC.

papers.title: Uncovering the Multifaceted Role of the Kinetochore Scaffold 1 (KNL1) in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Integrative Bioinformatics Analysis and CRISPR-Cas9 Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by pronounced heterogeneity, chromosomal instability, and limited therapeutic options. Kinetochore scaffold 1 (KNL1), a core mitotic checkpoint component, is implicated in multiple cancers, but its role in HCC remains unclear. Here, we integrated bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses with functional in vitro validation to elucidate the biological and clinical significance of KNL1 in HCC. KNL1 was markedly overexpressed in HCC tumors, particularly those harbouring TP53 mutations, and correlated with increased tumor break load, suggesting a link to structural chromosomal instability. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) and hallmark gene set enrichment identified a KNL1-associated G2M checkpoint network, in which KNL1 ranked among the top 10 hub genes. A KNL1-G2M network score, stratified patients into high- and low-score groups, with high scores correlates with poorer overall survival, increased proliferation, and higher chromosomal instability. Immune deconvolution (CIBERSORTx) revealed that high-score tumors were enriched in T-regulatory cells and M0 macrophages, and had elevated TIDE and exclusion scores, indicating potential resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Single-cell RNA-seq confirmed preferential activation of the KNL1-G2M module in malignant hepatocytes and highlighted increased extracellular matrix remodeling and immunomodulatory interactions. CRISPR-Cas9–mediated KNL1 downregulation in HepG2 cells induced modest G2/M arrest, suppressed proliferation, reduced survivin and Bcl2 expression, and produced ultrastructural changes consistent with early apoptosis. Collectively, our results implicate KNL1 and its associated G2/M network in tumor progression–related processes, including chromosomal instability, proliferative activity, and immune modulation in HCC. While further mechanistic and clinical studies are required, KNL1 and its associated network may represent a biologically relevant vulnerability and a potential biomarker of aggressive disease behavior in hepatocellular carcinoma.
