papers.title: Single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Cholesterol Metabolism Heterogeneity in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma and Identify NSDHL as a Key Regulatory Gene
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, and reprogramming of cholesterol metabolism plays a critical role in its malignant progression. However, the heterogeneity of cholesterol metabolism at the single-cell level and its key regulatory genes remain unclear. Methods This study integrated single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and bulk transcriptomic data (TCGA, GEO, ICGC) to systematically dissect the cellular landscape of cholesterol metabolism in PDAC. Malignant ductal epithelial cells were scored using five independent algorithms and divided into low (LCM), intermediate (ICM), and high (HCM) cholesterol metabolic subgroups. Cell communication, pseudotime trajectory, hdWGCNA, and XGBoost feature importance ranking were performed. Functional experiments including CCK-8, colony formation, EdU, wound healing, Transwell, and nude mouse tumor models were used to validate the role of NSDHL. Results Malignant ductal epithelial cells exhibited the highest cholesterol metabolic activity. The HCM subgroup showed enhanced communication with CAFs and endothelial cells, increased stemness, and coordinated activation of pro-tumor pathways (hypoxia, TNFα, NF-κB) and metabolic pathways (glycolysis, fatty acid synthesis). Pseudotime analysis revealed that cholesterol metabolism gradually increased along the LCM→ICM→HCM trajectory. Through hdWGCNA combined with XGBoost, NSDHL was identified as the most critical gene for the HCM phenotype. NSDHL was significantly overexpressed in PDAC tissues, enriched in high-malignancy regions, and correlated with poor prognosis. Knockdown of NSDHL significantly inhibited PDAC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, and delayed tumor growth in nude mice. Conclusion This study reveals the heterogeneity landscape of cholesterol metabolism in PDAC and identifies NSDHL as a key gene driving the HCM phenotype and malignant progression, providing a new theoretical basis for prognosis evaluation and targeted therapy of PDAC.

papers.title: Integrated single-cell transcriptomics reveal E2F1-driven multidrug resistance in medulloblastoma and identify Palbociclib as a therapeutic candidate
papers.abstract: Abstract Purpose Medulloblastoma (MB) is a malignant pediatric brain tumor where tumor recurrence driven by acquired multidrug resistance remains a paramount clinical challenge. Resolving the intratumoral heterogeneity underlying this resistance is urgently required to identify novel therapeutic targets. Methods Single-cell RNA sequencing data and large-scale bulk transcriptomes were integrated and comprehensively analyzed. Multidrug-resistant subpopulations were identified by mapping ridge regression-based drug sensitivity predictions to single-cell profiles. Developmental trajectories and core regulatory networks were reconstructed, and essential transcription factors were functionally evaluated by computational vector field perturbations. The prognostic value of specific cellular states was assessed, and potential therapeutic antagonists were screened using computational databases and spatial molecular docking. Results Two distinct multidrug-resistant reservoirs were identified, an E2F1 -driven DNA repair state exhibiting cross-resistance to genotoxic agents, and a ZIC5 -regulated neuronal differentiation state associated with Hedgehog signaling. Trajectory inference and in silico perturbations demonstrated that the continuous accumulation of E2F1 is critical for maintaining the chemoresistant DNA repair phenotype. Clinical deconvolution revealed that elevated E2F1 expression acts as a robust indicator of poor overall survival. Subsequently, computational pharmacogenomic screening and molecular docking identified palbociclib as a highly potent inhibitor capable of precisely binding and targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis. Conclusion An E2F1 -driven DNA repair program and a ZIC5 -associated differentiation state directly govern distinct multidrug resistance mechanisms in MB. Targeting the CDK4/6-E2F1 axis with palbociclib represents a promising precision therapeutic strategy to overcome chemoresistance in high-risk patients.

papers.title: smoothclust: Spatial smoothing and boundary-density summaries for spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the measurement of gene expression while preserving tissue organization. A common analysis task is the identification of spatial domains, defined here as spatially coherent regions with consistent expression profiles or cell-type mixtures and represented using categorical spatial tissue maps. However, while numerous methods have been developed to identify spatial domains, interpretable summary measures to quantify spatial domain organization and tissue architecture at the sample level remain less standardized. Here, we present smoothclust, a framework for spatial domain analysis consisting of two components: a spatial-smoothing-based clustering workflow for generating spatial domain labels, and a boundary density (BD) metric that provides local and sample-level summaries of label transitions on a spatial graph. Building on established categorical spatial statistics, the raw BD metric is calculated from the proportion of neighboring spatial locations that are assigned to different domain labels, and requires only spatial coordinates and domain labels as inputs. The metric can be calculated using either our spatial-smoothing-based domain labels or labels from external clustering methods or manual annotations. Relative BD is a composition-adjusted summary, calculated by dividing raw BD by its expectation under random relabeling with the observed label counts. By quantifying label transitions, our framework translates spatial domain label maps into interpretable local and sample-level summary measures of tissue architecture, facilitating exploratory analyses and comparisons across samples and biological conditions. We demonstrate the approach through evaluations across datasets from several spatial transcriptomics platforms and simulations. The spatial-smoothing workflow and BD metric are implemented in the smoothclust R package, which is freely available from Bioconductor and GitHub.

papers.title: Ground-truth evaluation of sparse autoencoder features on spatial, single-cell and language-model embeddings
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to extract interpretable features from the embeddings of biological foundation models. Because SAEs trained with different random seeds learn different features, reproducibility across seeds has become a common test of whether these features can be trusted. We asked whether reproducible features are also meaningful, using embeddings whose concepts are known: five spatial transcriptomics embeddings of two colorectal cancer sections and Geneformer embeddings of single-cell RNA profiles, with cell lineages as concepts; synthetic data with planted cell states; and the residual stream of a small language model, with token classes as concepts. Varimax rotations of the same embeddings were almost perfectly reproducible, yet rotation features (PCA, varimax and ICA) covered at most three of seven lineages and three of eight token classes. Single SAE fits showed the opposite profile: they covered most concepts with purer gene programs but reproduced only 27–46% of their features. A consensus over five SAE fits combined the two strengths. It was reproducible (78–98% across sources) and as pure as single fits: 11–40% of its features carried marker genes of another lineage, against 44–70% for varimax. Against the strongest baseline, varimax sparsified to the SAE’s sparsity, the consensus covered as many concepts on PCA and Geneformer embeddings and more on learned spatial and text embeddings. The consensus also had costs. It covered fewer lineages than single fits and, like all SAEs, missed weak planted states that rotations recovered; neither a longer single fit nor a second SAE trained on the consensus residual recovered what it discarded. Reproducibility alone therefore ranks features poorly: SAE features should be reported with the number of known concepts they cover and the purity of their gene programs, against a rotation of the same embedding sparsified to the SAE’s sparsity.

papers.title: NicheCorr: Identifying Niche-Specific Differential Gene Co-Expression in Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Cell–cell communication is central to biological processes such as immune responses and tumor progression, yet the role of spatial proximity between distinct cell types in shaping gene co-expression remains poorly understood. Existing approaches primarily identify differences in average gene expression across tissue regions, often overlooking how local cellular microenvironments reshape gene–gene interactions within cells. To address this gap, we introduce NicheCorr, a statistical procedure that identifies cell type–specific niche-associated gene co-expression changes within distinct spatial niches. In simulations, NicheCorr attained the highest power for detecting niche-dependent co-expression. It was also the only method evaluated that maintained Type I error control when mean expression varied nonlinearly with the niche, a setting in which CS-CORE, scHOT without mean adjustment, and the Pearson test all exhibited inflated false positive rates. Furthermore, NicheCorr integrates ligand–receptor (LR) inference, enabling a comprehensive view of spatially structured signaling interactions. We applied the framework to the CosMx SMI Human Liver FFPE Dataset and the Xenium Human Pancreatic Cancer Dataset, identifying 52 gene pairs in liver tumor cells whose co-expression changes with T-cell niche composition and 48 gene pairs in pancreatic cancer whose fibroblast niche–dependent co-expression differs between tumor and CFTR − tumor cells, and uncovering potential LR interactions that may underlie these differential co-expression patterns.

papers.title: Spatialsnake: a flexible workflow for spatial transcriptomics analysis across platforms
papers.abstract: Background Spatial transcriptomics technologies measure gene expression at different spatial resolutions and generate diverse data outputs. Existing workflows support a range of platforms and analyses, but combining methods and extending analyses to selected populations or tissue regions can require additional scripts and repeated data preparation. A common command-line interface supports single- and multi-sample analysis, with adjustable parameters and saved intermediate results. Users can select populations, tissue regions or distance-based neighborhoods, repeat clustering and annotation, and map refined labels back to the full dataset. Additional modules support cell-type composition estimation, spatial-domain identification, cell– cell communication inference, regulon analysis and sample-level comparisons. We demonstrate these functions using mouse-brain Visium and colorectal cancer Visium HD datasets. Joint analysis of three colorectal cancer sections retained 1,527,987 bins and enabled further analysis of 223,632 epithelial bins, linking epithelial subpopulation annotations to their locations within the complete tissue. Conclusions Spatialsnake provides a unified workflow for spatial transcriptomics analysis across sequencing- and imaging-based platforms. Its flexible analysis modules support both whole-tissue analysis and further investigation of selected cell populations and tissue regions.

papers.title: Single-cell-informed machine learning reveals prognostic and immune features of multiple myeloma
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Multiple myeloma (MM) is clinically heterogeneous, and the International Staging System (ISS) captures this heterogeneity only in part. We aimed to build a transcriptomic risk model anchored in single-cell and stage-associated gene expression, and to explore its immune context and therapeutic implications. Candidate genes were filtered by univariate Cox regression, and 101 combinations of 10 machine learning algorithms were benchmarked. The model was validated in three independent cohorts (GSE136337, GSE2658 and GSE4581) and examined with T cell subclustering, immune deconvolution, drug sensitivity prediction, genetic dependency data and molecular docking. Results Integration yielded eight candidate genes, five of which ( DLGAP5 , CENPF , PFDN2 , HNRNPF and MAP2K1 ) were associated with overall survival. High-risk patients had lower immune and stromal scores, higher TIDE scores and fewer predicted immunotherapy responders. Docking supported binding of risk-associated compounds to MAP2K1 . Conclusion This five-gene signature refines risk stratification beyond ISS, marks an immune-depleted high-risk phenotype and nominates MAP2K1 as a candidate therapeutic target in MM.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics tumor microenvironment determinants of tyrosine kinase inhibitor response in renal cell carcinoma: results from a phase 2 clinical trial.
papers.abstract: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) exhibits heterogeneous clinical outcomes, and limited biomarkers are available to predict response to targeted therapies. papers.title: Harnessing single-cell omics for farmed animal improvement and human health.
papers.abstract: Cellular heterogeneity underlies the regulation of complex traits and diseases, making cell-resolved molecular characterization fundamental for advancing precision agriculture and human biomedicine. papers.title: Benchmarking of cell type deconvolution techniques for microarray data.
papers.abstract: Cell type deconvolution algorithms have significantly advanced in recent years. papers.title: Alterations in the Immune-Fibrotic Axis Are Spatially Localized in the Aging Heart.
papers.abstract: The immune-fibrotic axis functions as a vicious feedback loop where age-related chronic, low-grade systemic inflammation (inflammaging) drives maladaptive tissue repair and fibrosis, while senescent fibrotic cells in turn amplify systemic inflammation. In the aging heart, immune dysregulation and fibroblast activation drive tissue scarring and stiffening and a higher risk of heart failure and vascular disease. The major biological significance of these findings is that cardiac immune-fibrotic remodeling is not a uniform, heart-wide process. Instead, it varies with cell type, with valves and aorta emerging as major sites where age-associated programs converge to progressively compromise cardiac structure and function.

papers.title: Identifying multi-omics spatial domains via masked autoencoder and diffusion-based latent regularization with SpaMEDM.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omics data provide complementary molecular views of tissue organization. However, their integration remains challenging due to data sparsity, technical noise, and modality-specific distributions. Here, we present Spatial Masked autoEncoder and Diffusion-based Model (SpaMEDM), an end-to-end graph representation learning framework that augments a dual-attention graph-integration backbone with masked reconstruction and diffusion-based latent noise-prediction regularization. In the masked track, randomly masked spot features are recovered by leveraging modality- and graph-specific neighborhood information. Furthermore, cosine-based paired-spot directional alignment and adjacency reconstruction encourage compatible cross-modality representations and preservation of the selected graph structure. SpaMEDM flexibly supports purely spatial, dual feature-spatial, and modality-specific feature-pruned spatial graph configurations. Evaluations across diverse spatial multi-omics datasets demonstrate competitive spatial-domain identification performance and produce integrated embeddings that facilitate downstream exploratory analyses.

papers.title: Post-transcriptional Regulation of FGF Signaling: Insights From Musculoskeletal System.
papers.abstract: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling plays a pivotal role in the development, maintenance, and regeneration of musculoskeletal tissues. papers.title: Glycolysis in pulmonary fibrosis: From drivers to therapeutic opportunities (Review).
papers.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a chronic and progressive interstitial lung disease with a poor prognosis and limited therapeutic options. Furthermore, therapeutic strategies targeting glycolytic enzymes and upstream metabolic checkpoints are highlighted, summarizing preclinical evidence for small‑molecule inhibitors and non‑coding RNAs as emerging regulators of glycolytic reprogramming. By consolidating current knowledge on glycolysis‑centric metabolic underpinnings of PF, this review underscores the promise of metabolism‑based interventions and discusses challenges for translating these findings into effective therapies.

papers.title: Single-probe, high-yield spatial mapping of diverse short RNA motifs
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has revolutionized our understanding of RNA biology. With SMOOTHY-FISH’s optimized single probe technique, short RNA motifs are converted into a new routinely measurable axis of spatial transcriptomics.

papers.title: Multi-omics, spatial omics and artificial intelligence in chronic diseases: current applications and future directions.
papers.abstract: Chronic diseases exhibit multiscale heterogeneity and spatial organization, yet analytical frameworks often fail to connect molecular perturbations, tissue architecture, and clinical outcomes within a unified evidence framework. Bulk and single-modality approaches can identify regulatory or cellular alterations but provide limited insight into why pathogenic programs emerge in anatomical regions, how they shape disease niches, and how they drive divergent clinical trajectories. Multi-omics partially addresses this gap by resolving interconnected layers of regulation, transcription, protein activity, and metabolism, whereas spatial omics maps these processes within preserved tissue architecture, enabling the delineation of lesion topology, interface states, and multicellular microenvironments. Artificial intelligence (AI) may further extend this framework by integrating molecular, spatial, imaging, and clinical data into disease representations that support disease stratification, the discovery of mechanistic patterns, and clinically testable predictions, provided that models are externally validated, biologically interpretable, and robust to dataset bias and domain shift. In this review, we examine how multi-omics, spatial omics, and AI can bridge the disconnect between molecular profiling, spatial pathology, and clinical translation in chronic disease research. We discuss six representative disease domains before synthesizing insights into how these approaches define molecular endotypes, map pathological niches, identify recurrent mechanistic patterns, and generate interpretable surrogate readouts for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment stratification. We also highlight limitations, including preanalytical variability, inconsistencies across platforms, limited external generalizability, and the challenges of translating high-dimensional outputs into deployable clinical tools. Finally, we outline priorities for scalable evidence systems, mechanism-guided validation frameworks, multimodal model interpretability, and prospective clinical implementation.

papers.abstract: Intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD) is accompanied by extracellular-matrix disruption, metabolic stress and immune-cell infiltration, but how metabolites mediate communication between disc cells and macrophages remains incompletely defined. papers.title: Spontaneous neuropathic pain.
papers.abstract: AbstractSpontaneous pain is a highly prevalent and disabling consequence of neuropathic disorders, yet it remains mechanistically underdefined and therapeutically underserved. Historically, preclinical animal models and clinical trials have been overwhelmingly biased toward stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity, relegating spontaneous pain to a secondary manifestation. Emerging evidence now challenges this view. Converging data from pharmacology, neural recordings, and systems-level causal manipulations indicate that spontaneous and stimulus-evoked pain arise from substantially dissociable molecular, cellular, and circuit substrates. Injured-fiber-derived ectopic activity within specific sensory neuron subtypes serves as a dominant peripheral generator of spontaneous pain, whereas cellularly distinct, intact spared-fiber pathways mediate stimulus-evoked hypersensitivity. At spinal and supraspinal levels, spontaneous pain preferentially engages affective-salience networks during pain chronification and may ultimately become stabilized within higher-order circuitry-while remaining dynamically coupled to afferent input. This mechanistic delineation carries critical translational implications. Current diagnostic and treatment guidelines rarely differentiate symptom domains, and most therapies have been validated primarily using stimulus-evoked or overall pain intensity endpoints-potentially contributing to a mechanism-therapy mismatch and variable efficacy. We argue that spontaneous neuropathic pain should be defined as a separate symptom domain rather than considered as a spontaneous manifestation of evoked pain mechanisms. This recognition demands longitudinal, biomarker-informed phenotyping to capture its persistent and fluctuating nature, and thereby enable robust mechanistic dissection at peripheral, spinal, and cortical nodes. Reframing spontaneous neuropathic pain along these lines will provide a foundation for precision therapeutics that target defined cell types, specific molecular drivers, and maladaptive network states-enabling mechanism-based, symptom-aligned treatments.

papers.abstract: Pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant therapy is associated with favorable outcomes in breast cancer, yet differences in response cannot be explained by immune-cell abundance alone. Translation into clinical practice will require standardized spatial definitions and measurements, reproducible assessment of organized immune structures, subtype- and regimen-specific validation, and demonstration of added value beyond established pathological indicators. papers.title: Beyond breathing: Lung as a sensory organ.
papers.abstract: The lung, one the largest branching organs in our body and vital for survival at first breath, is commonly known as the gas exchange organ. Recent novel findings on lung sensing cells, molecules, and lung-brain crosstalk in the emerging discipline of interoception have highlighted the consideration of the lung as a sensory organ. Acknowledging the central importance of lung sensing to human health and disease, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute convened a workshop to synthesize the past, current, and future of lung sensing research, with in-person presentations by approximately 20 interdisciplinary experts and a large virtual audience. Here, we highlight the key topics discussed and summarize a blueprint for the future in this important field.
